name: Dante Alighieri
role: Florentine poet and political writer (1265-1321); prior of Florence, exiled 1302
summary: In De Monarchia Dante argues that peace and justice require one universal temporal monarch whose authority comes directly from God and not through the Pope, and that the Roman people won empire by right. He holds that the Church should not hold temporal power, a view repeated in the Divine Comedy, while keeping each kingdom's own laws in its particular affairs.

clerical-rule.rationale: De Monarchia III denies that the Church has any power to bestow or hold temporal authority, and in Purgatorio XVI he says the joining of sword and crozier ruins both.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Book III of De Monarchia argues that the authority of the emperor comes directly from God, not from the Pope or the Church.

natural-rulers.rationale: In De Monarchia I he endorses the saying that those strong in understanding are the natural rulers of others and that the one best fitted to rule can best order the rest.

person-over-state.rationale: In De Monarchia I he says the monarch, like any consul, is the servant of the citizens in respect of the end of government, and that men are most free when they exist for their own sake.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: In De Monarchia I he argues that nations and kingdoms should be ruled by one supreme monarch in matters common to all, while keeping their own laws for their particular needs.

notes: A first audit. Answers rest on De Monarchia (words); the Divine Comedy and Il Convito were read for statements and add little beyond it, since the poem's moral judgments of persons in the afterlife are not positions on laws. Themes searched: government, society, world, liberty, economy, means. Dante's exile and condemnation in 1302 is not a record on any statement.
